catalog_locator: Section 5.9.2 'Prosody: word structure', p. 359; section 5.8.6 'Tonal changes', p. 353; restated at pp. 380 and 383 and summary table p. 84.
catalog_quote: The answer to that question is that Malieng is clearly an iambic language in word-structure. Morphemes of more than one syllable consist of a presyllable with limited phonological contrasts, followed by a main syllable. Compounds tend to be lexicalised into sesquisyllabic structures likewise. [p. 359] ... The second type of tonal change is conditioned by the word structure of Malieng. The iambic prosody of Malieng generates a tendency to arrange disyllabic words, binary compounds, binary phrases (for instance, preposition+noun), among other binary forms, into sesquisyllabic structure. Within this sesquisyllabic structure, the stress is borne in the second element (i.e. the main syllable), which preserves its original tonation category. The first element is lenited both segmenally and suprasegmentally, becoming toneless (indicated with a superscript 0). ... (18) kuoA1 ‘day’ + ɣɤkD1 ‘after (time)’ > kuo0 ɣɤkD1 ‘tomorrow’ > ku0.ɣɤkD1 ‘tomorrow’ [p. 353]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Malieng is a tonal ('tonation': 5 tonal categories x 2 phonation registers) language whose words are monosyllables or iambic sesquisyllables; in any polysyllabic word or lexicalised compound the stress falls on the final (main) syllable, which alone carries tone, while the preceding presyllable is unstressed, reduced and toneless.
new_statements.exceptions: Coordinate compounds tend to keep a full disyllabic form (p. 383), and sesquisyllabised compounds are realised as full disyllables in careful/didactic speech; sentence-final particles may change tonal category (intonation). No tone sandhi reported. No exceptions to iambic word prominence are stated.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (and, per the author, also phrase-level 'iambic' structure, e.g. preposition+noun binary phrases reduced to sesquisyllables). Section 5.9.2 is explicitly labelled by the author as 'almost just a placeholder' answering whether disyllables are iambic or trochaic; no instrumental stress study.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement source (Badosa Roldós 2025) describes Malieng / Mã Liềng of Hà Tĩnh and Quảng Bình provinces, Vietnam (author gives ISO 639-3 'pkt or bgl'; ~1,250 speakers, six villages); Glottolog lists Malieng and Mã Liềng as alternative names of male1282 (Maleng), so the match is direct, although Wikipedia notes that Chamberlain 2003 / Sidwell 2009 treated 'Malieng' as a Chut [scb, chut1247] dialect while Babaev & Samarina 2021 group Mã Liềng with Maleng. The secondary source Ferlus 1997 describes Maleng Brô, the Laos variety (Kha Phong / Maleng Kari cluster, Khammouane), also under male1282 per the Wikipedia/Babaev-Samarina dialect list.

sources.note: States Kri has NO lexical tone; instead a rime-level two-way register contrast (heavy = breathy, lower pitch, raised vowels vs light = tight/clear) cross-cut by a three-way 'terminance' contrast (voiced, voiceless, checked), giving six rime types 'structurally and historically comparable to tones' and likened to the pre-tonogenetic stage of Vietnamese/Muong; register is independent of initial consonants (section 2.3.2); no instrumental study, auditory impression that heavy register has lower pitch (p. 30); explicitly warns Kri is not 'transitional' or archaic (p. 41).

sources.note: The abstract states that Kri Phoong of Vietnam is a sesquisyllabic tonal language, and that having tones is the main difference from the Kri of Laos, which has none. It says nothing about stress, so the entry's fixed-01 (iambic) stress kind is untouched; the tone class tone-and-stress is confirmed for the Vietnam variety and refined by the tonal-vs-toneless split between the Vietnam and Laos varieties.
